title: Strings
summary: Work with text, compare it safely, and avoid the == trap.
refresher: A Java `String` is text stored as an **object**. Use **methods** like `.length()` and `.substring()` to work with it. Use `.equals()` to compare text. `==` checks whether two **variables** point to the same object, which is not the same question.

sections.title: Text values and joining
sections.summary: Create Strings, call basic methods, and join text safely.

blocks.body: A **String** holds text. It can be one word, a full sentence, or an empty string. In Java, String is an **object**, so you use a dot to ask it questions or call **methods** on it.
Java has primitive types like `int`, `double`, `boolean`, and `char`. **String** is different: it is an **object**. That is why you call methods on it with a dot, and why text comparison needs care.
blocks.caption: The dot calls **String** **methods**. length counts characters. toUpperCase makes a new uppercase String.

This is the wrapper every Java program needs. Later examples show only the statements that go inside `main`, and you can assume this **class** around them. Note the capital S in `String`: it is capitalized because it is an **object** type, while `int` is lowercase because it is a primitive.
blocks.body: The big beginner trap is comparison. If you want to know whether two **Strings** contain the same letters, use `.equals()`. Do not use `==` for text equality.
`school.length()` is a **method** call. The dot asks the String object for something. The parentheses matter because you are calling the method, not reading a variable.
blocks.caption: The wrong version asks whether both **variables** are the same **object**. The right version asks whether the text matches.

blocks.title: Java catches type errors before it runs anything
blocks.body: **Strings** do not change in place. A **method** like `trim()` or `toLowerCase()` returns a new String. Save that result if you want to keep it.

blocks.caption: The `+` sign joins **strings** together. This is concatenation. When one side is a String and the other is a number, Java converts the number to text for you, which is why `"Score: " + 10` works and gives you text.

sections.title: Indexes and common methods
sections.summary: Read characters and substrings without stepping past the end.

blocks.caption: The **methods** you will reach for most. `charAt(i)` gets one character, and counting starts at 0. `substring(a, b)` takes the characters from a up to but not including b. `substring(a)` with one number runs from a to the end.

blocks.title: StringIndexOutOfBoundsException
blocks.body: `Bears` has five characters, so the valid **indexes** are 0 through 4. Index 5 is past the end. When you see StringIndexOutOfBoundsException, count the characters and subtract one to find the largest valid index.

blocks.why: `word.length()` is 5, so this asks for `word.charAt(5)`. The legal **indexes** stop at 4, so nothing lives at 5 and the program halts on that line with a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. "It prints s" is the answer that pulls at you, and for a fair reason: the letter s does sit at the end of the word. Its **index** is 4, though, not 5, because the count opened at 0. Reach it with `word.charAt(word.length() - 1)`. The code does compile, since the compiler has no way to know what that number will be before the program runs.

sections.title: Compare text by content
sections.summary: Use equals for text and understand why == is the wrong question.

blocks.body: Now the part that matters most in this whole lesson. Sooner or later you will compare two **Strings**, and Java gives you two things that look like they do that job. Only one of them asks the question you actually have in mind.

blocks.caption: `==` asks whether two names point at the same **object** in **memory**. `.equals()` asks whether two **strings** contain the same characters. When you compare text, the second question is the one you meant. The left version compiles cleanly

blocks.body: Both strings contain `yes`, but `==` may still say false because it compares object identity. Use `.equals()` when you care whether the text matches.

blocks.title: The `==` bug is quiet, and sometimes it looks like it works
blocks.body: Use `.equals()` every time you compare **String** text. `==` may seem to work for text typed directly in code, but it can fail for text from input or from joining strings. Nothing crashes; the branch just goes the wrong way.

blocks.why: `b` is built at runtime by joining `a` with "202", so it is a brand new **object** that happens to hold the same characters as the "cs202" written in the code. `==` compares the two objects, sees that they are not the same one, and prints false. `.equals()` compares the characters, finds them identical, and prints true. If you picked "true then true", you read `==` as a question about the text. It is a question about the object, and that gap is exactly where the bug lives.

sections.title: String method results
sections.summary: Keep returned strings because String values do not change in place.

blocks.body: One more idea ties the rest together. A **String** is immutable: once it exists, its characters can never be changed. So no String **method** edits the string you called it on. Each one builds a new String and hands it back, and if you do not catch what it hands back, it is gone.

blocks.caption: The first `toUpperCase()` builds an uppercase **string** and drops it on the floor, because nothing was told to keep it. `name` is untouched. The second line stores the result back into `name`, which is what you almost always want.

`trim()` strips whitespace off both ends, the first thing to do with keyboard **input**. `split()` cuts a **string** into an **array** of pieces at the separator you name. Look at the third number: `raw` is still 16 characters long. `trim()

blocks.title: A String method call on its own line is usually a bug
blocks.body: `name.trim();` by itself trims a copy and then throws that copy away. Store the result, print it, or test it. Otherwise the original string has not changed.

sections.title: Check string habits
sections.summary: Carry the text-comparison and method habits into practice.

blocks.title: Habits that save you hours
items: Save the result of **methods** that **return** a changed **String**.
Check **indexes** carefully; Java starts counting at 0.

strings-lesson-check-1.title: Length is not the last index
strings-lesson-check-1.body: String positions start at 0, so the count is one past the final valid index.
strings-lesson-check-1.notice: A five-character string uses positions 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4.
strings-lesson-check-1.mistake: Do not use the length itself as an index unless you mean one past the end.

strings-lesson-check-2.title: Follow each string operation
strings-lesson-check-2.body: When several string methods appear together, trace the returned value from left to right before choosing the output.
strings-lesson-check-2.notice: Some methods return strings, and some return collections of smaller pieces.
strings-lesson-check-2.mistake: Do not keep measuring the original text after a method has returned a different value.

strings-summary-01.title: Strings are text values
strings-summary-01.body: A **string** stores text. You can measure it, read characters by position, take pieces from it, and build new text from it.
strings-summary-01.notice: Most string operations return a value; they do not rewrite the original text in place.
strings-summary-01.mistake: Do not treat the character count as the final valid position.

strings-supplement-01.title: Strings do not change in place
strings-supplement-01.body: Many beginner bugs come from trying to edit one character inside a string. Instead, build a new string with the change you want.
strings-supplement-01.notice: Immutable means the original text value is not edited directly.
strings-supplement-01.mistake: Do not assign into a string index like it is a list slot.

strings-authored-01.title: Convert before joining text and numbers
strings-authored-01.body: Joining text with a number needs an explicit conversion or a formatted string. That makes the intended output clear.
strings-authored-01.notice: The plus operator can mean different things depending on the values around it.
strings-authored-01.mistake: Do not expect the language to always guess whether plus means addition or text joining.

strings-authored-02.title: Index errors come from bounds
strings-authored-02.body: If code asks for a string position that does not exist, the bug is usually a zero-based counting mistake.
strings-authored-02.notice: Check both the string length and the position being requested.
strings-authored-02.mistake: Do not read the final character before checking that the string is nonempty.

strings-authored-03.title: Use the method result
strings-authored-03.body: A string method call often gives back transformed text. Store, return, print, or compare that returned value.
strings-authored-03.notice: Calling the method alone may do nothing visible.
strings-authored-03.mistake: Do not assume a string method changed the variable automatically.

strings-authored-04.title: Reach the final character safely
strings-authored-04.body: To read the last character, use the language's last-index pattern and first make sure the string has at least one character.
strings-authored-04.notice: Last-index shortcuts are convenient, but empty strings still have no last character.
strings-authored-04.mistake: Do not use the count as the final index.

strings-authored-05.title: Slices stop before the end
strings-authored-05.body: A slice or substring range usually includes the start and stops before the ending position.
strings-authored-05.notice: The stop value acts like a boundary, not a character to include.
strings-authored-05.mistake: Do not count the stop position as part of the returned text.

strings-authored-06.title: Normalize typed text before comparing
strings-authored-06.body: When people type answers, spaces and capitalization can vary. Clean the text before comparing when exact formatting is not the point.
strings-authored-06.notice: Normalize both the value and the comparison target in the same way.
strings-authored-06.mistake: Do not clean only one side of a comparison and leave the other side inconsistent.
